paras: The arrest of a railroad labor agent at Canton, Mississippi, took place in August 1920, when local authorities arrested an unnamed Black man employed by the Illinois Central Railroad to secure labor. According to the Chicago Whip, he was held incommunicado after a "mock trial" and fined $500, to be worked out on a peonage farm. The Whip presented the case as an attempt to stop Black migration from the state and reported that people were leaving Canton by night in response.

The Whip's dispatch described Canton as a town "known for its peonage farm environments" that had "again been brought into disrepute." It called the working out of fines on peonage farms "the usual system of the South" and a main cause of the migration of thousands of Black people to the North.

The dispatch, datelined Canton, August 18, said the authorities had arrested a "prominent colored man" whose job was recruiting labor for the Illinois Central Railroad. No charge is given in the report. After what the Whip called a "mock trial," he was fined $500 and held incommunicado, and his name was withheld from the public. The paper said the fine would be worked out on one of the state's peonage farms.

The Whip reported that "it is said" numbers of people were leaving Canton by night as a result of the affair. No report of the prisoner's release, an appeal, or any official inquiry appears in the coverage.

The only account found ran in the Chicago Whip on August 21, 1920, under the headline "Labor Agent Kidnaped." Although the text describes an arrest and a trial, the headline treated the detention as a kidnaping, and the paper called the prisoner a "victim" of authorities "anxious" to keep "our people" from leaving the state. The Whip used the case to connect peonage in the South with the northward migration.
No white newspaper report of the arrest was found in the coverage, and no other Black paper carried the story.

accounts.label: Black correspondent (Canton dispatch)
accounts.gist: Canton authorities, anxious to keep Black people from leaving the state, arrested an Illinois Central labor agent, gave him a mock trial and a $500 fine to be worked out on a peonage farm, and held him incommunicado; people were said to be leaving Canton by night.

framing.detail: The Chicago Whip headlined the arrest 'Labor Agent Kidnaped', called the trial a 'mock trial', the agent a 'victim', and said Canton had 'again been brought into disrepute' for its peonage farms.

record_check.dossier: On or before 1920-08-18 (dispatch dateline); the arrest date itself is not given
The article names only Canton, Miss.; no county is stated
One unnamed Black labor agent of the Illinois Central Railroad (name withheld)
No charge is stated; the Whip ties the arrest to his recruiting labor for the Illinois Central

record_check.record: Residents reportedly began leaving town at night.
record_check.dossier: The Whip says 'it is said' that 'numbers are leaving Canton by night'; in context these are Black residents ('our people')

info: On or before August 18, 1920 (dateline of the dispatch); exact date of the arrest not given
One unnamed 'prominent colored man' employed by the Illinois Central Railroad to secure labor; his name was withheld from the public
'the authorities in this community' (Canton); no officials named
Fine of $500 to be worked out on one of the state's peonage farms; prisoner held incommunicado

sources.note: 'Labor Agent Kidnaped': Canton, Miss., Aug. 18 dispatch; unnamed Black Illinois Central labor agent arrested, held incommunicado after 'mock trial', $500 fine to be worked out on a peonage farm; people leaving Canton by night.
quotes: The city of Canton, known for its peonage farm environments has again been brought into disrepute by the arrest of a prominent colored man
So anxious are the authorities in this community to prevent our people from leaving the state that they are holding their victim incommunicado after a mock trial and a fine of $500.00.
It is said that as a result of this affair, numbers are leaving Canton by night now.

set_aside: South Dakota news column; 'Canton' here is Canton, S.D. (a pharmacy board appointment); unrelated.
